n: Job continues: his spirit is broken, his life is snuffed out, and the grave is waiting for him.

f.g: Extinguished, put out like a lamp.

n: He is surrounded by mockers, and he must keep watching their taunting.
Job asks God himself to put up a pledge for him, since no human friend will. He is asking God to guarantee his innocence.

f.g: A guarantee or bond posted for someone.
Shake hands on a deal — to become someone’s guarantor.

n: God has closed the friends’ minds to understanding, Job says, so he will not let them triumph.

f.g: Blinded their minds — they cannot see the truth of Job’s case.

n: Job quotes what sounds like a proverb: whoever betrays friends for gain will see his own children suffer. It warns the friends against their disloyalty.

f.g: Likely “denounces friends for a share of their property” — a betrayal of friendship.

n: God has made Job a proverb people use for misery. Once he was honored; now people spit in his face.

f.g: A saying or by-name for disgrace.
A small drum; but the Hebrew here likely means “one in whose face they spit.”

n: Grief has dimmed his eyes, and his body has wasted away to a mere shadow.
Job says upright people should be appalled at how he is treated and stirred against the godless.
A ringing statement of resolve: the righteous will keep to their path, and those with clean hands grow stronger and stronger. Job will not give up his integrity.
Job challenges his friends to come back and try again, because he has not found a single wise man among them.

f.w: I cannot find one wise man among you

n: His days are over and his plans are broken off — even the deepest desires of his heart.

f.g: Literally “possessions of my heart” — his cherished hopes.

n: His friends try to call his night day, offering cheerful promises of light when Job sees only darkness.

f.w: They change the night into day

n: All Job can look forward to is the grave as his home and darkness as his bed.

f.g: Hebrew sheol — the place of the dead.

n: Job speaks of decay as his family — calling corruption his father and the worm his mother and sister. He is at home only with death.
Where, then, is his hope? Who can see any hope left for him?
Job’s hope seems to go down with him into the gates of the grave. Even so, he will soon reach for a greater hope in chapter 19.

f.g: The gates of sheol, the realm of the dead.

f.w: rest together is in the dust
